finding.claim: The server never enforces Config::max_auth_attempts (default 10) or tracks a rejection limit. auth_attempts and AuthRequest.rejection_count are incremented but never compared, so a client can make unlimited USERAUTH attempts on one connection. The only brute-force control is the per-request rejection delay (~1 guess/sec/connection by default).
finding.source: Unauthenticated network client that completes the SSH transport handshake and sends repeated USERAUTH_REQUEST (password, publickey, keyboard-interactive, none) messages.
finding.sink: handler.auth_password / auth_publickey / auth_keyboard_interactive credential checks (encrypted.rs:562, 604, 641, 783 region).

trace.note: max_auth_attempts declared as the 'maximal number of allowed authentication attempts'
self.common.auth_attempts += 1 after each userauth message; no comparison against config.max_auth_attempts
auth_request.rejection_count += 1 in reject_auth_request; field never read anywhere in the crate (auth.rs:236)
tokio::time::sleep_until(until) is the only throttle; no disconnect or lockout follows

finding.guards_checked: Config::max_auth_attempts: declared and defaulted but unused (grep of whole tree). rejection_count: written, never read. Per-request constant-time rejection delay: present, limits rate only, not total attempts. No lockout, no disconnect path keyed to failure count. Connection-level limits are out of scope and were not reviewed.

finding.claim: Unbounded counter i for pty-req terminal modes leads to an out-of-range slice &modes[0..i] when more than 130 mode entries are sent. This panics the session task. The modes array is [_;130] and only the write is guarded by i<130, while the increment is unconditional.
finding.source: Authenticated client's pty-req channel request with a mode string containing more than 130 five-byte entries (up to the inbound packet size limit).
finding.sink: &modes[0..i] slice at encrypted.rs:1201, passed to handler.pty_request.

trace.note: mode_string = Bytes::decode(r); length bounded only by the packet
loop while mode_bytes non-empty; code==0 terminates; each iteration consumes 5 bytes
if i < 130 guards only modes[i] = ... write; the else branch just logs
i += 1 runs on every iteration regardless of the guard, so i can reach 131+ (also counts unknown codes)
&modes[0..i] with i > 130 panics: range end out of bounds

finding.guards_checked: mode_bytes.len()<5 check (1151); code==0 length check (1146); ensure_end(r) (1175); write-side i<130 guard (1159). No cap on i before the slice. Precondition: the pty-req arrives on an authenticated session (or on a server that accepts auth_none). Impact is panic of the connection task; process-wide impact only if the build uses panic=abort or the task runs unguarded.

finding.claim: Certificate authentication trusts any certificate whose self-signature verifies. russh does not check that the signing CA is trusted, that the cert type is user (not host), that valid principals include the login name, or critical options. Those checks are left to the application's auth_openssh_certificate, whose doc comment ('signature verified and key ownership confirmed') reads as if a trust check had happened. The default implementation rejects, so this is exploitable only when an application implements auth_openssh_certificate without its own CA and principal checks.
finding.source: Attacker-supplied certificate blob in a USERAUTH_REQUEST publickey message, self-signed with the attacker's own CA key and carrying the attacker's key as the certified key.
finding.sink: handler.auth_openssh_certificate(user, cert) at encrypted.rs:782, which grants authentication for the requested user.

trace.note: PublicKeyOrCertificate::decode parses the certificate from the attacker-controlled blob
cert.verify_signature(): checks only that the cert is signed by the signature_key embedded in the cert itself (self-consistency), not by a trusted CA
Verifier::verify of the session-bound request signature with the certified key (proves possession of that key)
handler.auth_openssh_certificate(user, cert) invoked; application must perform CA, principal and cert-type checks here
default auth_openssh_certificate returns Auth::reject(), so the default is safe

finding.guards_checked: Expiry check (encrypted.rs:702-711). Self-signature check (714). Possession-of-key signature over session_id + request (774). Default reject (mod.rs:296). Not performed by russh: CA allowlist, cert_type == user, valid_principals contains user, critical-option enforcement. Verdict is PLAUSIBLE: a library API footgun, not a default-open bypass.
